children.text: Sharm el-Sheikh is often discussed only as a beach resort.
Hotels, pools, seaside restaurants, and all-inclusive holidays are a big part of this town. Ending there wastes Sharm a little.

The town sits at the southern tip of the Sinai Peninsula, facing the sea where the Gulf of Aqaba meets the Red Sea. Offshore are world-rated coral reefs; behind are southern Sinai mountains and desert. Going inland connects to Mount Sinai and the St. Catherine area.
To travel Sharm well, use it as a resort while seeing the sea and desert properly.
See the sea at Ras Mohammed
The biggest reason to visit Sharm el-Sheikh is the Red Sea underwater world. At its centre is
Ras Mohammed National Park
at the southern tip of the Sinai Peninsula.

Ras Mohammed is known as Egypt's first designated national park. A protected area including sea and land, it protects coral reefs, mangroves, desert landform, and habitats of seabirds and fish. A day trip from Sharm, it lets you feel sea density completely different from resort beaches.

For divers, Shark Reef and Yolanda Reef are well known. Currents in places allow seeing pelagic fish and rich coral walls. Certified divers, choosing sites matching experience, can enjoy Red Sea-clear visibility and vertical drops.

For non-divers, Ras Mohammed has plenty of value. Boat snorkelling, shallow underwater observation, and tours including land-side scenery offer options matching stamina and age. Without swimming confidence, rather than going far offshore, enjoying with life vest and guided range reassures.

At coral reefs, basics — don't touch, don't stand, don't chase. Red Sea coral remains comparatively healthy in places; affected by tourism pressure and water temperature change. Sunscreen, fin use, boat entry — traveller behaviour leaves on the environment.
Ras Mohammed isn't only for photos. It is the best place to understand why Sharm developed here.
Strait of Tiran and boat trips
Northeast of Sharm is the Strait of Tiran dive area. Reefs like Jackson, Woodhouse, Thomas, and Gordon are popular with experienced divers.

Currents can strengthen; not always beginner-suited. Underwater landform beauty is a big appeal; for diving, judge by certification, dive count, and day's sea conditions. Good dive centres pick safety-fitting sites, not only customer requests.
Snorkelling boat trips vary in ease by sea conditions. With small children or weak swimmers, confirm boat facilities, guide count, life vest provision, and lunch and shade in advance.
In Sharm, choosing cheap tours isn't always a gain. Equipment condition, staff explanation, safety management, and participant count differences show directly in sea experience quality.
Naama Bay
and beach use
Naama Bay developed as Sharm el-Sheikh's tourism centre. Hotels, restaurants, cafés, dive centres, and seaside promenade gather — an easy-to-move place for first stays.

The beach has organised facilities, with eating and resting easy, so convenient for families and first Red Sea trips. For quiet nature, can feel a little commercial. Early morning is comparatively calm with sea and town easier to see.

Sharks Bay, Ras Um Sid, and around El Fanar have shore-entry snorkelling areas. Hotels and beach clubs often manage access; if using beaches other than your accommodation's, confirm day-use conditions in advance.

Sharm coastlines aren't all freely accessible the same way. Resorts, public beaches, beach clubs, jetties, and coral-protected areas mix. When choosing a stay, beyond room size, confirm sea access to fail less.
Going to the desert
Sharm's appeal isn't only the sea. Behind the coast spread dry southern-Sinai mountains and wadis. At sunset, heading inland greatly changes the resort impression.

Many desert tours offer ATV, jeep, camel rides, and stargazing. Content varies. Some take photos in short time; some let you touch landform, water sources, plants, and life knowledge with Bedouin guides.

South Sinai's Bedouin community knows the land as a place of life, not a tourism backdrop. Good tours respect that knowledge. Whether they show only "desert-like staging" or convey reading of the place matters.
For desert, evening into night fits. You avoid day heat and enjoy rock-mountain colour change and stars. Even winter nights cool; carry a light layer to reassure.
Considering Mount Sinai and St. Catherine

About several hours inland from Sharm sit Mount Sinai and St. Catherine. A place where religious, historical, and natural-landscape meanings layer — one of the most important southern Sinai destinations.

Mount Sinai has been tied to Moses in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions. Many travellers climb at night, see sunrise at the summit, and descend. Less serious climbing and more long mountain walking, walked in dark, with altitude, cold in winter. Walking shoes, warm clothing, water, and light essential.

St. Catherine's Monastery was built in the 6th century under Justinian I — one of the world's oldest monasteries. Still a functioning religious community, not just a tourist facility. Even when visiting, time, dress, photography, and accessible places have limits.

This area's visit conditions can change by local regulations, monastery situation, religious events, and security judgment. With plans during Sharm stay, confirm both before departure and on arrival via trusted operators or public information.
Mount Sinai and St. Catherine are less light additional activity and more a stamina-using day. Between beach holidays, plan to rest the next day.
See old town and Naama Bay apart
Sharm el-Sheikh isn't a town made of one centre. Naama Bay developed for tourism, walkable with easy food and tour arrangement.
Around Sharm el-Maya old town has more of a local-life atmosphere. Markets, port, mosques, and daily shops — sides of the city hard to see from resort alone.

Al-Mustafa Mosque has a strong exterior impression and is sometimes lit at night. When visiting, be aware it is a place of worship; consider dress and photography. A Coptic Orthodox church also exists, recalling Sharm isn't only a town for foreign travellers but an Egyptian town with the religious life of residents.
Stay in Naama Bay, eat and walk in the old town, head to sea and desert. Combined that way, Sharm becomes a place beyond resort surface.
Choosing a dive centre
Sharm has many dive centres. With many options, don't decide by price alone.
Confirm — courses and guidance following international certification, equipment maintained, participant experience properly checked, safety briefing thorough, and ratio not too high.
For intro diving, shallow depth, clear explanation, and judgment not pushing matter. With weak swimming, children, or returners, tell from the start. Good operators don't treat it as a bother.
For certified divers, don't take Red Sea visibility lightly to underestimate currents. At parts of Tiran and Ras Mohammed, day-condition changes difficulty. No need to force above-experience sites.
When to go
Sharm el-Sheikh travels year-round; period suits vary by activity.

To enjoy both sea and desert, October to April is workable. Comparatively gentle temperatures ease day movement and desert tours. European winter-holiday timing crowds; consider hotels and popular tours early.
Summer has good sides for entering water; land heat strengthens. Desert tours, old-town walking, and Mount Sinai direction movement need careful time and stamina.
For diving and snorkelling, beyond season, wind, waves, tide, and visibility affect. Don't fix plans to one day; margin to choose good sea days reassures.
Safety and travel information
Sharm el-Sheikh accepts many travellers as Egypt's major Red Sea resort. The Sinai Peninsula varies greatly by area; don't treat South Sinai resorts and North Sinai the same.

Before travel, confirm your government's travel information. US State Department and others publish Egypt-wide cautions plus strong warnings on North Sinai and some areas. For resort stay, national park, and inland tours, follow local regulations and operator judgment.
At sea, safety management decides trip quality. Don't dive on unwell days, don't swim after alcohol, don't stand on coral, observe boat assembly times. Basic care greatly reduces risk.
In the desert, avoid solo movement, carry water, prepare for night cold. For mountain or monastery, road regulations, permits, and local-guide need can change; don't move on personal judgment.
The best use of Sharm
Sharm el-Sheikh suits doing-nothing holidays too. The town's real strength is switching between rest and adventure.
Morning at sea. Afternoon resting at hotel. Evening walking old town or Naama Bay. Another day heading to desert. With stamina, a day for Mount Sinai or St. Catherine.
That pace suits Sharm.

Seen only as resort, Sharm can look like one of similar seaside destinations. With Ras Mohammed's underwater walls, southern-Sinai rock peaks, Bedouin land knowledge, and religious-history weight together, this place becomes a far deeper destination.
Sharm el-Sheikh is a place to rest at the sea. At the same time, beneath the sea and inside the desert, another trip begins.

deck: A practical guide to Sharm el-Sheikh — beyond beach resort, as the sea of Ras Mohammed, southern Sinai desert, and the entry to Mount Sinai.
